name: llm_requirement_coverage_defaults
description: Managed default guidance for LLM requirement coverage decomposition behaviour.
lines: For requirement_coverage: semantically decompose capability and qualification requirements into atomic items. Return legal or formal entry gates separately in eligibility_requirements.

Every requirement_coverage and eligibility_requirements item must include a decomposition object: decomposition.operator is exactly one of single, and, or; decomposition.elements is a non-empty list of atomic parts. eligibility and qualification rows are always decomposition.operator=single with exactly one element.

For an atomic requirement, use decomposition.operator=single with exactly one element whose text mirrors the requirement, whose canonical_concept is one short reusable concept name suitable for a candidate profile (e.g. "NV2", "Australian Citizenship", "CBAP", "Java"), and whose canonical_fact_resolved reflects your confidence. For a single row, set the row-level canonical_requirement to that same element.canonical_concept.

canonical_requirement and element.canonical_concept must each name one concept only. Never copy requirement prose such as "NV2 Security Clearance Required" or a compound alternatives phrase such as "CBAP, Agile BA, or equivalent certifications are desirable" into either field.

If one ad sentence contains multiple independently testable concepts the candidate must all meet (an AND relationship, e.g. 'hold a clearance and a degree'), emit them as separate atomic requirement_coverage items, each decomposition.operator=single, rather than one combined row. This applies especially to named tools/platforms in an AND list: each independently required tool is its own single row, even when the candidate profile has one existing combined capability label that mentions more than one of those tools. Match each atomic row to whatever existing profile fact proves it; leave only the genuinely unproven tool/fact as not_shown. Use decomposition.operator=and (one row, one element per concept) only for a genuinely inseparable conjunctive phrase you cannot split into independent rows; leave the row-level canonical_requirement empty in that case.

When a clause instead offers alternatives joined by 'or' — such as a list of acceptable certifications, acceptable degree fields, or acceptable tools ('Microsoft Purview or BigID') — emit exactly one requirement_coverage item with decomposition.operator=or and one element per named alternative. Give each element its text, and its canonical_concept plus canonical_fact_resolved=true when that alternative is itself a clean reusable concept. Leave the row-level canonical_requirement empty. Do not emit a separate row per alternative and do not invent a generic umbrella label (e.g. "Data Governance Tool") to summarise the group.

Do not use decomposition.operator=or for optional examples, preferences, or narrower subdomains when the clause still has one clear core fact. Use operator=single with that core fact as the one element, and keep the optional examples only as context. For example, "experience in financial services, ideally banking or insurance" has the single reusable core fact "Financial Services Experience": emit operator=single with one element whose canonical_concept is "Financial Services Experience" and canonical_fact_resolved=true.

When one sentence explicitly gives different preference strength to a narrower domain and a broader fallback, you MUST preserve that ranking as separate atomic requirements (each operator=single) and MUST NOT collapse them into one broader requirement. Exact example: 'Previous experience within insurance is highly desirable, with broader financial services experience also well regarded.' MUST emit two rows: Insurance Experience with importance=strongly_preferred, and Financial Services Experience with importance=preferred. Match each row independently to profile evidence. The narrower fact may also substantively satisfy the broader fact.

Example of AND decomposition into separate rows: "write testable user stories and acceptance criteria for AI features, including evaluation metrics and guardrails" names two independently testable concepts — user stories/acceptance criteria authorship, and AI evaluation/guardrails — emit them as two operator=single rows, not one combined row. Example of an OR clause: "Azure DevOps and Miro (or equivalent)" — Azure DevOps is one atomic independently required tool (its own operator=single row); "Miro (or equivalent)" is its own operator=or row with an element "Miro" (canonical_concept "Miro", canonical_fact_resolved=true) and an element "equivalent whiteboarding tool" (canonical_concept empty, canonical_fact_resolved=false).

decomposition.elements lists the atomic parts of the clause: for operator=or, one element per acceptable alternative; for operator=and, one element per independently required concept that could not be emitted as its own row; for operator=single, exactly one element mirroring the row. Do not add extra elements just because a requirement mentions a proper noun.

Set element.canonical_fact_resolved=true only when element.canonical_concept is a genuinely resolved, reusable profile concept you are confident in — not the ad wording restated, and not a guessed umbrella label. Set it false whenever canonical_concept is empty, uncertain, or itself echoes the requirement/matched_job_text wording. For operator=single this flag gates whether the candidate can be offered a profile-learning action on the row; for operator=or it gates the per-branch Add action. Treat it as a strict confidence judgement, not a formality.

Keep element.canonical_concept and element.canonical_fact_resolved internally consistent: a clearly resolved atomic concept must have canonical_fact_resolved=true even if the original sentence also contained optional examples or preferences.

Set element.capability_judgement to: "capability" when the element names a reusable capability or qualification concept; "uncertain" when you are not confident it is a clean reusable concept; "non_capability" when it is not a reusable concept at all (a bare responsibility clause, restated ad wording, or boilerplate). Base this only on the element wording; it is not a way to flag mixed requirement types.

Even when element.capability_judgement is "non_capability", still provide element.canonical_concept and element.canonical_fact_resolved whenever a smallest defensible reusable concept genuinely exists. A mandatory requirement is never dropped; a resolved concept lets it stay actionable, and an optional non_capability element is retained for analysis rather than shown on the card.

A body or organisation name inside a qualification clause (e.g. IIBA, PMI, ARITA) names who issues or certifies a credential, not a credential itself. Do not treat the body name as its own qualification or requirement_coverage item unless the ad explicitly requires a fact about the body itself, such as membership of it.
Do not put a whole sentence as a single item; split compound sentences into their atomic parts.

Decompose a mixed sentence into its atomic parts BEFORE classifying each part. Classify each atom independently for requirement_type and requirement_kind. Example: 'ability to work through ambiguity, manage complexity and deliver projects' becomes three rows — 'work through ambiguity' and 'manage complexity' are requirement_kind=behavioural_expectation, while 'deliver projects' is requirement_type=capability, requirement_kind=professional_capability and is scored normally.

On every requirement_type=capability row set requirement_kind. Use requirement_kind=behavioural_expectation for generic personal-conduct, disposition, mindset, or attitude wording: working autonomously or with minimal supervision, self-motivation, 'excellent communication skills' stated as a personal trait, adaptability or flexibility, resilience, attention to detail, proactiveness, curiosity, strong work ethic, positive attitude, team-player disposition, willingness or eagerness to learn, and willingness or openness to embrace or use new technology including AI tools. These rows stay visible as employer context but are never scored, never a profile gap, and never a learning signal.

Always set requirement_kind explicitly to one of the two allowed values on every requirement_type=capability row. A capability row returned with a missing, empty, or unrecognised requirement_kind is treated as unclassified: it is held aside, never scored, never a profile gap, never a learning signal, and never actioned, and it is never defaulted to professional_capability. Only a row you explicitly classify as professional_capability is scored.

Use requirement_kind=professional_capability for observable professional skills, activities, domains, tools, and deliverables — including interpersonal ones performed as a professional activity such as stakeholder facilitation, negotiation, workshop facilitation, requirements elicitation, team leadership, and running governance forums. When wording is a concrete professional activity, it is professional_capability even if it also implies a soft skill.

'Willingness to use AI', 'comfortable adopting AI tools', or 'embrace AI in your workflow' is a behavioural_expectation. Never record it as an AI development, AI engineering, machine-learning, or prompt-engineering capability, and never emit a canonical_concept for it.
requirement_kind applies only to requirement_type=capability rows. Leave it unset for eligibility and qualification rows.

For each atomic requirement: assign the weakest accurate importance. Use mandatory only when the ad explicitly says required, must, essential, mandatory, or similar hard-block language. Use strongly_preferred for emphatic non-mandatory preference language such as highly desirable or strongly preferred. Use preferred for ordinary desirable/preferred/highly regarded/well regarded language. Use bonus only for explicitly optional, nice-to-have, or bonus language. Do not mark every row mandatory.
Store the original job-ad sentence in matched_job_text for traceability — do not match the whole sentence directly to a capability.

A job title, role title, or seniority label the candidate has held (including any family from the supplied role experience matrix) proves only explicit role-family and duration facts. On its own it never proves a generic professional capability, a behavioural_expectation, autonomy, judgement, stakeholder management, or a named tool or platform — each of those needs its own explicit candidate evidence. Never put a bare role title in matched_candidate_fact for a capability row.

A covered_requirement_elements entry must be a real multi-word fragment of the requirement wording, never a single generic word such as "AI", "data", "digital", "systems", "platform", or "delivery". One shared generic token between the requirement and the candidate evidence is not a substantive element and does not make a match supported or partially_supported.

Use requirement_type=capability or requirement_type=qualification in requirement_coverage. Use requirement_type=eligibility in eligibility_requirements. Qualification covers education, degrees, certifications, and formal qualifications. A deterministic check still validates existing capability and eligibility mappings, but qualification interpretation is LLM-driven.
capability covers skills, responsibilities, knowledge, domain experience, seniority, and years or duration of experience — e.g. '5+ years supporting client outcomes' is capability, not eligibility.

eligibility covers legal entry gates such as citizenship, work rights, security clearances, licences, and registrations — e.g. 'ability to obtain a Baseline security clearance' is eligibility. Qualification covers education, degrees, certifications, and formal qualifications.

Preserve eligibility specificity with requirement_subtype. Use the managed eligibility subtype vocabulary supplied in the prompt; for example, a security-clearance gate stays requirement_type=eligibility with requirement_subtype=clearance rather than becoming a separate top-level type. Leave requirement_subtype empty for capability and qualification rows.

Return every explicit eligibility gate in eligibility_requirements, one independently testable gate per item. Eligibility requirements are additional to requirement_coverage and must never be omitted to make room for capability or qualification rows. Do not duplicate eligibility rows in requirement_coverage.

When an ad states two or more distinct eligibility conditions joined together (e.g. 'hold a security clearance and be an Australian citizen'), emit one eligibility_requirements item per condition, each decomposition.operator=single and matched independently to its own profile eligibility fact — do not merge them into a single item that needs one combined fact to match.

A citizenship, permanent residency, or existing work-rights/visa eligibility fact in the profile satisfies a requirement worded as work authorisation, work rights, or the right to work in that country — match it to that fact instead of leaving matched_candidate_fact empty just because the wording differs.

A requirement that states a duration or years of experience in a field, tool, or role is capability even if the field itself sounds formal (e.g. years of experience in a regulated industry is still capability, not eligibility).

For every explicit duration or years-of-experience requirement, return experience_components that decompose the wording into short fragments with kind duration, role_or_activity, or qualifier. A qualifier is any substantive domain, industry, technology, methodology, product, environment, or other constraint beyond the duration and role/activity. For every component also return profile_supported and profile_evidence. profile_evidence must be concise evidence from the candidate profile that supports that component; leave it empty when profile_supported=false.

Role history can validate the duration and role/activity portion only. It must never be used as evidence for a qualifier. For each qualifier, profile_supported=true only when the candidate profile directly substantiates the full substantive qualifier. Shared geography, a broader parent industry, an adjacent domain, or generic occupation experience is not enough to prove a narrower qualifier. If support is uncertain, set profile_supported=false and profile_evidence=[] instead of inferring support. A requirement with qualifier components is supported only when candidate profile evidence supports every qualifier; if no qualifier is supported, use not_shown even when role history meets the duration. Use partially_supported only when candidate evidence proves at least one substantive qualifier or when the complete substantive content is supported but the duration is insufficient.

On the duration component (or the role_or_activity component) of an explicit years/months requirement, set matched_role_family to the single name from the supplied role experience matrix that most precisely matches what the requirement is asking for time in. When the requirement asks for time in the role or activity in general, return the canonical matrix family name that carries the combined history — its listed title variants are part of that same family's accumulated history. When the requirement asks specifically for time under a narrower exact job title that the matrix lists as a title variant (for example 'Senior Business Analyst' when the matrix family is 'Business Analyst'), return that title-variant name exactly as the matrix shows it and do NOT substitute the parent family name: only tenure actually held under that exact title defensibly proves that requirement. Leave matched_role_family empty when no matrix family or listed variant can be safely tied to the requirement. Deterministic code then does the month arithmetic and comparison — the whole family history for a family-name match, only that variant's own listed months for a title-variant match — and an empty value leaves the row for human review rather than asserting a pass or fail. Never write the number of years back into canonical_requirement or any profile concept — the duration is compared against captured role history (refreshed from the CV/onboarding), not stored as a profile fact.

For a requirement whose core is a duration or years of experience, canonical_requirement and element.canonical_concept must name only the underlying role, skill, or domain concept and must never contain a number of years or months (write "Business Analysis", never "5 Years Business Analysis").

Link capability requirements to the exact profile capability name, eligibility requirements to the exact profile eligibility fact, and qualification requirements to the exact profile qualification name.

Use matched_candidate_fact for the matched profile fact and keep capability_name / eligibility_name aligned with the requirement_type. On each element, use element.matched_candidate_fact for the profile fact that matched that specific element.
Leave matched_candidate_fact empty only for not_shown or mismatch items.
Keep each requirement_coverage or eligibility_requirements item compact: short phrases only for requirement, matched_job_text, matched_candidate_fact, and profile_support.
Within requirement_coverage, prefer the most important atomic requirements when the ad is long. Never omit an explicit eligibility_requirements gate for this prioritisation.
Do not mark a requirement supported or partially_supported merely because the candidate has a broadly transferable capability. Transferability is not requirement evidence.
A supported or partially_supported match must prove at least one substantive element stated in the requirement itself. Return those exact job-requirement fragments in covered_requirement_elements.

If the profile only shows a broad parent capability but does not show the defining domain, technology, activity, qualification, methodology, or responsibility, use not_shown and leave matched_candidate_fact empty.

Examples of invalid partial matches: agile delivery does not prove investment appraisal or ROI; general business analysis does not prove banking experience; policy interpretation does not prove complaints, fraud, or case-management experience.

Set role_defining=true ONLY for specialist domain, platform, profession, or subject-matter requirements that distinguish this role from routine generic duties of its occupation. Mandatory generic duties such as stakeholder engagement, requirements elicitation, process mapping, agile delivery, generic reporting, or generic data analysis are NOT role-defining by themselves. All requirements that belong to the same specialist focus MUST use exactly the same short role_defining_group label, even when one is a domain capability and another is a specialist platform. Do not create separate role_defining_group labels for closely related facets of one specialization.
